Chief Complaint: Right wrist pain Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure: None HPI: Ms. is an year old woman with a history of osteoarthritis and psoriasis who presents with acute onset right wrist pain. The patient developed pain in the right wrist on the evening of . This made it difficult to sleep. The pain was associated with swelling and erythema with decreased range of motion in the and digits. She took one oxycodone with minimal relief. The wrist increased I swelling over the course of . She denies fevers, chills. She has no trauma or wound in the area. She has a history of OA in the left wrist but this is significantly different. Pertinent ED course (including exam, Hospital Course: Ms. is an with a history of OA and psoriasis, who presented with acute onset R wrist pain found to have positively birefringent rhomboid crystals consistent with pseudogout. Septic joint was ruled out with negative culture. Patient was treated with a dose of IV methylprednisolone and NSAIDs with clinical improvement. ACUTE ISSUES Right wrist pain: Pseudogout: Joint aspiration revealed positively birefrigent crystals consistent with pseudogout. Fluid had numerous WBCs concerning for septic joint, however remained negative for bacterial growth. Patient was given 20mg IV methylprednisolone x 1 and naproxen to treat acute flare, which responded with decreased swelling and erythema. Patient also presented with a peripheral leukocytosis of 11.9 which downtrended aside from an acute increase following IV steroids. She was seen by hand surgery who recommended elevation of the RUE during her hospitalization. She was discharged with a soft wrist splint and ortho follow up. CHRONIC ISSUES Psoriasis: Stable. Patient was continued on home c PMH: Psoriasis Osteoarthritis Multiple small bowel obstructions

Chief Complaint: R leg pain Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure: ORIF tibial plateau Hospital Course: The patient presented to the emergency department and was evaluated by the orthopedic surgery team. The patient was found to have right tibial plateau fracture and was admitted to the orthopedic surgery service. The patient was taken to the operating room on for external fixator and fasciotomies, on for fasciotomy closure and for definitive fixation, all of which the patient tolerated well. For full details of the procedure please see the separately dictated operative report. The patient was taken from the OR to the PACU in stable condition and after satisfactory recovery from anesthesia was transferred to the floor. The patient was initially given IV fluids and IV pain medications, and progressed to a regular diet and oral medications by POD 1. The patient was given antibiotics and anticoagulation per routine. The patient's home medications were continued throughout this hospitalization. The patient worked with who determined that discharge to home was appropriate. The hospital course was otherwise unremarkable. PMH: HTN, HLD, presents with the above fracture s/p mechanical fall. States he was working on his boat stepping down from stepladder when the ladder fell; pt landed directly onto L knee. Immediate pain and inability to bear weight. No HS, no LOC. Sustained some superficial abrasions to R ankle and R knee. No pain in ankle. No numbness, tingling, paresthesias. no subjective weakness though limited by pain. Went to in then transferred here. Physical Exam: O: RLE: Dressings c/d/i Able to wiggle Toes. SILT at level of toes. Normal ankle ROM. Foot is warm and well perfused.

Chief Complaint: Right upper and lower limb weakness Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure: Cyber Knife to brain lesion HPI: Mr. is a pleasant HTN, DL, Asthma, T2DM, RA, and poorly differentiated penile SCC s/p partial penectomy w/ rapid met recurrence s/p C3 TIP who p/w RLE weakness x days. He acutely developed RUE weakness while walking up the stairs at 6PM tonight and fell back and hit his head. He called EMS and code-stroked by EMS. He was seen by neurology and found to have preserved strenght in the RUE but RLE weakness w/ R foot drop and sensory changes. NCHCT revaled a large hypodensity in the L frontoparietal region w/ c/f mass. He was seen by who advised dex and no AEDs. He denied any headache, changes to vision, no N/V, no other acute complaints. Hospital Course: Mr. is a HTN, DL, Asthma, T2DM, RA, and poorly differentiated penile SCC s/p partial penectomy w/ rapid met recurrence s/p C3 TIP who p/w RLE/RUE weakness and a fall, found to have new brain lesion, concerning for metastatic disease or second primary tumor. TRANSITIONAL ISSUES [ ] Continue dexamethasone 4 mg BID until follow up with neuro-oncology. This was tapered from TID as of evening. His insulin needs will fluctuate with this taper. His insulin is being decreased by 30% to accommodate this change, but will likely need further adjustment in insulin based on his sliding scale needs. [ ] Discharge diabetes regimen: - Continue Lantus 25 units QHS - Continue Humalog 12 units AC breakfast, Humalog 10 units AC lunch and Humalog 8 units AC supper - Continue sliding scale to start at 200 mg/dL 2 units+2 units/50mg/dl - Metformin 1000 mg daily [ ] Continue PPI and Bactrim for prophylaxis while on steroids. [ ] Continue Keppra for seizure prophylaxis. [ ] Recommend rechecking electrolytes in 1 week to assess hyponatremia. Chief Complaint: L arm pain with changing L proximal humerus enchondroma Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure: Resection L proximal humerus chondrosarcoma and reconstruction with APC. HPI: Mr. is a very pleasant gentleman with Ollier's disease. He has had significant involvement of his left upper extremity and right lower extremity for many years. In the recent past, he was being evaluated for a finger enchondroma with Dr. . This was somewhat concerning for risk of malignancy and so he had that removed, but in the workup for that, he had a bone scan. This revealed increased activity compared to the other enchondromas with a lesion in his left proximal humerus. He had an MRI of that area. On followup MRI, it seemed that the cartilaginous neoplasm in his right proximal humerus was quite a bit larger, especially with a component that was posterior to the glenoid and so concern was definitely raised about chondrosarcoma and he is now coming here for further treatment and evaluation. He has been under Dr. Dr. care at and is now coming here for further orthopedic oncology care as he is now adult age. He does have pain in his left shoulder that is related to lack of motion. It is better when he has some movement in it and changes position. It bothers him a lot at sleep because of that. It wakes him up at rest from a deep sleep, the pain is about a and with activity it is mo Hospital Course: Mr. was admitted to the hospital following resection of L proximal humerus chondrosarcoma and reconstruction with APC. Pre-operatively an intra-scalene nerve catheter was placed by APS and a foley was placed prior to the operation. He was placed in a sling post-operatively with instructions for no AROM/PROM of the shoulder. On POD 1 foley was removed and he was voiding independently. On POD 2 nerve catheter was removed. His hospital course was otherwise uneventful. On POD 2 he was tolerating PO, pain controlled on PO medications, voiding independently, and passing gas. He was deemed appropriate for home discharge at this time. Physical Exam: NAD, AOx3 Resp: Breathing comfortably on RA Cardiac: RRR, no MGR LUE: Dressing c/d/i. No erythema or drainage. In sling SILT ax/r/u/m distribution Motor intact elbow flexion/extension, wrist flexion/extension, EPL, FPL, IO. 2+ radial pulse.

Chief Complaint: planned admit for of disopyramide and monitoring of QTc Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure: None HPI: woman with obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, HFpEF, obstructive sleep apnea on CPAP, obesity s/p bariatric surgery, found to have worsening LVOT on TTE , and admitted on for planned disopyramide initiation to reduce the degree of LVOT. She was first seen in heart failure clinic in after she was noted to have a murmur during evaluation prior to bariatric surgery and echocardiogram revealed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Cardiac MR in was consistent with HCM with basal anteroseptal wall measuring 1.6 cm but no LGE present. Her peak LVOT gradient at that time was 24 mmHg which increased to 53 mmHg in . For the last few years, she has baseline class IIIa functional capacity with exertional dyspnea after walking for less than a block on flat ground. She has been taking maximum doses of metoprolol and diltiazem to medically manage the LVOT. She presented for routine heart failure clinic follow up on and underwent echocardiogram which showed worsening of the LVOT to 80 mmHg. She is admitted from home for initiation of disopyramide. She is at her baseline functional status today which included intolerance to exercise but no shortness of breath at rest. No chest pain, palpitations, or Hospital Course: Outpatient Providers: TRANSITIONAL ISSUES Discharge wt: 258.38 lb Discharge Cr: 0.8 [] Patient provided 4 doses of disopyramide on discharge due to retail pharmacy unavai Physical Exam: ADMISSION EXAM VS: Temp: 99.2 PO BP: 114/73 R Sitting HR: 69 RR: 20 O2 sat: 95% O2 delivery: RA GENERAL: Well developed, well nourished in NAD. Chief Complaint: Rash Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure: None Hospital Course: male with history of bladder , PE, and current Waldonstroms macroglobulinemia who is presenting with rash consistent with disseminated shingles. ACUTE ISSUES: Disseminated Zoster: Patient presented with lesions that appeared on his left anterior shin and scatterd along his back. These lesions appeared one day prior to presentation and were confirmed to be Zoster on this admission via DFA. Given his immunocompromised status, he was treated with IV acyclovir with good tolerance ( ) and transitioned to oral valacyclovir on discharge (1g TID for total 10 day course, to complete . His shingles is complicated by neuropathic pain in his left leg and back, for which he was given Tylenol and gabapentin. Back pain: Patient presented with lower back pain, which is almost resolved. This occurred in the context of recent muscle strain and is reproducible, and he had no systemic signs to suggest abscess. CHRONIC ISSUES: Waldonstroms macroglobulinemia: Dx in , treatment started in when he received retuxin and dexamethasone. In he was found to have ophthalmologic signs of hyperviscosity, so he received 4 cycles of bendamustine with the final 2 cycles administered with rituximab (completed in . App PMH: of bladder , PE, Waldonstroms macroglobulinemia presenting with rash. Patient states that his pain left sided back pain began around 10 days ago and gradually worsened after attempting to lift his wife and assist her with her ADLs. He denies any trauma or falls. He denies any weakness or numbness. He denies any saddle anesthesia. He denies any incontinence of urine or stool. He does state that yesterday he noted a temperature of 100 degrees F and that has been after taking fairly consistent NSAIDs. Chief Complaint: Foul smelling urine, nausea/vomiting, RUQ pain Major Surgical or Invasive Procedure: None HPI: M DM/ESRD s/p combined kidney/pancreas TPX ( ), recent admission for cholecystitis s/p cholecystectomy, p/w foul smelling urine, nausea/vomiting, and persistent RUQ pain. Patient reports that since his cholecystectomy 3 weeks ago he has had persistent RUQ pain. He also states that since his foley was removed on that shortly afterwards he began to develop chills and difficulty urinating. He would dribble, have some flow, then dribble again, and feel like he did not fully empty his bladder. Took some alleve last night which helped his chills but otherwise has not tried anything else. This morning, his legs felt rubbery and his urine had a bad smell. (He had his gf look at it since he is legally blind, and no abnormal color or blood seen.) He also felt bad reflux and nausea, with dry heaving for 10 minutes. He drank some water which he later vomited up. This prompted him to come to the ED. He denies ha, fever, cp/sob, cough, diarrhea. In the ED, initial vitals were: 99.5 82 130/74 16 97% RA - Hospital Course: s/p kidney/pancreas transplant in , presenting with complicated UTI after recent admission for cholecystitis and cholecystectomy requiring Foley on discharge. UTI, COMPLICATED: Presenting with urinary difficulty, foul smelling urine, leukocytosis and UA positive for infection. Complicated given anatomy and immunosuppression, with recent Foley catheter. Treated with empiric cefepime which was narrowed to ciprofloxacin PO for 2-week total course. Urine culture with pansensitive EColi. Blood cultures negative. Well appearing throughout hospitalization. URINARY RETENTION. Recent stricture dilation by Urology. Relieved with Foley catheter. Given history of reported BPH symptoms, we started him on finasteride 5mg daily. He was discharged home with a Foley catheter in place with outpatient Urology followup. S/p kidney/pancreas transplant: Transplant US normal. Continued home cyclosporine 75mg daily, azathioprine 50mg daily and prednisone 5mg daily. Osteoporosis: secondary to long-term steroid use. Cont home bisphosphonate. HTN. Stable. Cont home dilt and HCTZ. HLP. Stable. Cont home pravastatin. Patient tells me that she has been in and out of hospitals for the past several months, but had been doing fairly well since her discharge from in . She attended a PHP at and then one at . This ended last week. Over the past week, her depressive symptoms got worse and "the suicidal thoughts came back." She clarifies that she deals with SI chronically, but usually the thoughts are "fleeing". She has been thinking off and on this past week about killing herself. She attributes this to being home alone without structure; she feels that weekly outpatient appointments are not sufficient. She did not tell her therapist or boyfriend how bad things were. Her boyfriend has her psych meds in a lockbox, and she has been compliant with them. Yesterday she "impulsively" overdosed on all the medications she could; these were OTC meds (Tylenol and Advil) and the meds that are PRNs that she has access to (hydroxyzine and rizatriptan). She reports depressio Hospital Course: 1. LEGAL & SAFETY: On admission, Ms. signed a conditional voluntary agreement (Section 10 & 11) and that legal status remained in place throughout admission. Ms. was also placed on 15 minute checks status on admission and remained on that level of observation throughout while being unit restricted until 2 days prior to discharge when it was determined to be safe for her to go on fresh air walks. . 2. PSYCHIATRIC: ) Review of OMR as well as interview indicated that patient has a history of impulsive self-harm prior to previous admissions, suggestive of persistent difficulties with distress tolerance, emotion regulation, and effective coping skills. She continued to present with a flat, restricted affect, and linear communication with denial of SI/HI/AVH. . Diagnostically, her presentation was concerning for ongoing affective decompensation, likely MDD. Given the seriousness of Ms suicide attempt as well as ongoing evidence of affective decompensation, difficulty engaging with outpatient treaters, recent history of multiple prior suicide attempts, and demonstrated superficiality in engaging with safety planning, Ms. appeared to be at acutely elevated risk of self-harm. . Patient tells me that she has been in and out of hospitals for the past several months, but had been doing fairly well since her discharge from in . She attended a PHP at and then one at . This ended last week. Over the past week, her depressive symptoms got worse and "the suicidal thoughts came back." She clarifies that she deals with SI chronically, but usually the thoughts are "fleeing". She has been thinking off and on this past week about killing herself. She attributes this to being home alone without structure; she feels that weekly outpatient appointments are not sufficient. She did not tell her therapist or boyfriend how bad things were. Her boyfriend has her psych meds in a lockbox, and she has been compliant with them. Yesterday she "impulsively" overdosed on all the medications she could; these were OTC meds (Tylenol and ibuprofen) and the meds that are PRNs that she has access to (hydroxyzine and rizatriptan). She reports depressio Hospital Course: 1. LEGAL & SAFETY: On admission, Ms. signed a conditional voluntary agreement (Section 10 & 11) and that legal status remained in place throughout admission. Ms. was also placed on 15 minute checks status on admission and remained on that level of observation throughout while being unit restricted until 2 days prior to discharge when it was determined to be safe for her to go on fresh air walks. . 2. PSYCHIATRIC: ) Review of OMR as well as interview indicated that patient has a history of impulsive self-harm prior to previous admissions, suggestive of persistent difficulties with distress tolerance, emotion regulation, and effective coping skills. She continued to present with a flat, restricted affect, and linear communication with denial of SI/HI/AVH. . Diagnostically, her presentation was concerning for ongoing affective decompensation, likely MDD. Given the seriousness of Ms suicide attempt as well as ongoing evidence of affective decompensation, difficulty engaging with outpatient treaters, recent history of multiple prior suicide attempts, and demonstrated superficiality in engaging with safety planning, Ms. appeared to be at acutely elevated risk of self-harm. . The followin PMH: Diagnoses: major depressive disorder, anxiety/PTSD, borderline PD Hospitalizations: multiple, most recently Deaconess4 in Current treaters and treatment: Prescriber is NP , therapist Medication and ECT trials: Cymbalta, Zoloft, Geodon, Prazosin, hydrochloride, Seroquel, Wellbutrin, Celexa, lamotrigine, venlafaxine, Neurontin Self-injury: several prior SAs by OD , , h/o superficial cutting Harm to others: denies Access to weapons: denies .
